stories.title: Scanning for SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-31324 webshells continues, per SANS ISC honeypots

writeup.what_happened: SANS ISC reported on 9 November 2026 that its honeypots are receiving requests for webshell paths such as ant.jsp under the SAP NetWeaver /irj/servlet_jsp/irj/root/ directory, along with requests to the vulnerable metadata uploader endpoint. These requests are tied to CVE-2025-31324, an unauthenticated file upload flaw rated CVSS 10.0. According to SANS, one source address (82.26.72.21) is probing a broad list of upload and webshell paths across many products, including SharePoint, Joomla extensions, Samsung MagicInfo and WhatsUp Gold, alongside SAP. SANS frames the activity as attempts either to exploit NetWeaver or to find webshells that earlier attackers already planted.
writeup.why_it_matters: CVE-2025-31324 is in CISA KEV, has public proof-of-concept code and an EPSS of 99.5%, so any unpatched internet-facing NetWeaver Visual Composer instance should be assumed at risk or already compromised. Scanners checking for existing webshells means earlier compromises can be reused by new actors, so patching alone is not enough without a compromise check. The same scanner also targets SharePoint and other upload endpoints, which may be present on edge-facing Windows servers.
recommended_actions: Apply SAP's security fix for CVE-2025-31324 to all NetWeaver systems, prioritizing those reachable from the internet, or block access to the /developmentserver/metadatauploader endpoint until patched.
Inspect the /irj/servlet_jsp/irj/root/ directory and related NetWeaver web directories for unexpected .jsp, .java or .class files and treat any found as a compromise.
Review web server and reverse proxy logs for requests to the metadatauploader endpoint and to ant.jsp or other unknown JSP files, and for traffic from 82.26.72.21.
Hunt for shells or reconnaissance commands spawned by the NetWeaver Java server processes.
If a webshell is found, isolate the host, rotate SAP service and connected credentials, and investigate lateral movement.

stories.title: CISA adds exploited GPUStack, OpenSSH, FreeSWITCH and IBM Aspera Faspex flaws to KEV

writeup.what_happened: On 9 November 2026 CISA added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. According to CISA, CVE-2026-102895 in GPUStack lets an unauthenticated attacker gain administrative access, create persistent admin API keys, expose worker and cloud-provider secrets, and execute code through the inference-backend import endpoint. CVE-2026-123158 is an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on Linux, and CVE-2026-116779 is a code injection flaw in SignalWire FreeSWITCH that can lead to credential disclosure, call control and command execution. CVE-2026-123218 in IBM Aspera Faspex lets an authenticated user bypass authorization and escalate privileges. The sources do not name affected or fixed versions or describe the attackers.
writeup.why_it_matters: All four flaws are confirmed exploited and carry a federal remediation due date of 12 November 2026. The OpenSSH bypass is the broadest exposure: it affects internet-facing Linux servers and appliances, has public proof-of-concept code and an EPSS of 16.5%. GPUStack AI servers, FreeSWITCH VoIP systems and Aspera Faspex file-transfer portals are often exposed to the internet, and exploitation can hand over full control or leak cloud credentials (EPSS 0.6%, 2.2% and 0.7% respectively).
recommended_actions: Inventory internet-facing Linux hosts running OpenSSH and apply the vendor or distribution fix for CVE-2026-123158 by 12 November 2026. Until patched, restrict SSH to VPN or allow-listed source addresses.
Patch or take offline any exposed GPUStack, FreeSWITCH and IBM Aspera Faspex instances according to vendor guidance, and block internet access to GPUStack and FreeSWITCH management interfaces.
On GPUStack, review admin accounts and API keys for unexpected creation, revoke unknown keys, and rotate worker and cloud-provider secrets stored in the platform.
On FreeSWITCH, rotate SIP and configuration credentials, and review the host for unexpected child processes and call-routing changes.
Follow CISA's forensics triage expectation: check each affected system for signs of compromise from before the patch, not only after it.

sources.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
CVE-2026-123158: OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability
CVE-2026-116779: SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability
CVE-2026-123218: IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

hunting_steps: Use Defender Vulnerability Management to list devices exposed to the four CVEs, then confirm against your external asset inventory for systems Defender does not cover.
Identify Linux hosts accepting inbound SSH from public IP addresses and prioritize them for patching.
On GPUStack and FreeSWITCH hosts, look for shells, download utilities or interpreters launched by the service process.
Review GPUStack audit data for new administrator users or API keys created by sources you do not recognize.
Review Aspera Faspex user roles for unexpected privilege changes since late October 2026.

The available reporting does not describe how ARARA was compromised, when the breach happened, or whether any data beyond email addresses was taken.

The sources give no indicators or technical details to hunt for.
recommended_actions: Warn users that SEGA-branded emails asking for logins, payment details or account verification may be phishing tied to this breach.
Watch email security reporting for a rise in SEGA-themed phishing and add sender or URL blocks as concrete lures show up.
Review your own third-party marketing and newsletter providers to confirm what subscriber data they hold and how they will notify you of a breach.

stories.title: France attributes October attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems to Iranian state-backed hackers

writeup.what_happened: According to BleepingComputer, France has attributed cyberattacks in October to Iranian state-backed hackers. The attacks disrupted refrigeration systems at more than 700 supermarkets and other retail sites. French officials say they caused food losses and at least 15 fires. The report does not name the affected vendors or products, and it does not describe how the attackers got in or which techniques they used.
writeup.why_it_matters: This is a confirmed state-backed operation that caused physical damage through building and refrigeration control systems, which often sit outside normal IT security monitoring. Organizations with remotely managed HVAC, refrigeration or building-management controllers, especially in retail, may face similar risk. No technical indicators or vulnerabilities have been published, so defenders currently have nothing specific to hunt for.
recommended_actions: Inventory refrigeration, HVAC and building-management controllers and their remote-access paths, and remove any direct internet exposure.
Require MFA and allow-listed access for vendor and third-party remote management portals and VPNs that reach these systems.
Replace default or shared credentials on OT controllers and management interfaces.
Segment building and OT networks from corporate IT and restrict inbound management traffic to defined jump hosts.
Watch for technical details or indicators released by French authorities and apply them to hunting once they are available.

stories.title: Huntress details AhsayCBS backup server intrusions with webshells, cryptominers and a Python implant

writeup.what_happened: Huntress has published a follow-up analysis of intrusions against AhsayCBS backup servers. According to Huntress, attackers exploited the servers and left hidden webshells, a second cryptocurrency miner, and a Python-based command-and-control implant tied to the specific compromised host. The available summary does not name a CVE, the initial access vector, affected versions or indicators of compromise.
writeup.why_it_matters: Backup servers hold copies of sensitive data and often have broad network access and stored credentials, so a foothold there threatens both data and recovery capability. Huntress reports in-the-wild exploitation, but no patch or affected version range is identified in the sources, so defenders should treat internet-facing AhsayCBS instances as potentially compromised until checked.
recommended_actions: Inventory AhsayCBS servers and remove direct internet exposure of the management web interface, or restrict it to trusted IP ranges, until Ahsay guidance is confirmed.
Check AhsayCBS web application directories for unexpected or recently modified script files such as JSP pages that could be webshells.
Hunt for shells, scripting interpreters or Python processes started by the AhsayCBS service, and for sustained high CPU usage indicating miners.
Review Ahsay vendor advisories and apply any available AhsayCBS updates.
If compromise is found, rebuild the server, rotate credentials stored on or used by it, and verify backup integrity.

explainer.concept: Webshells: persistent backdoors planted through web server vulnerabilities
explainer.dek: A webshell is a small script file dropped into a web application's served directory that lets an attacker run commands on the server by sending ordinary HTTP requests to it.
explainer.why_today: SANS honeypots show attackers still hunting for SAP NetWeaver webshells planted through CVE-2025-31324, and Huntress found hidden webshells left on exploited AhsayCBS backup servers. In both cases the webshell outlives the original flaw.

parts.heading: How a webshell works
paragraphs: A webshell is a script in whatever language the server executes, such as JSP on Java application servers, ASPX on IIS, or PHP on many Linux stacks. Once it sits in a directory the server serves, any HTTP request to its path makes the server run it with the privileges of the web application process. A typical webshell takes a command or file operation from a request parameter, runs it, and returns the output in the response.

Attackers usually plant webshells by abusing an unauthenticated file upload, a path traversal, or a code execution bug. CVE-2025-31324 is the textbook case: the SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer metadata uploader accepted files without authentication, and attackers used it to write JSP files into the portal's servlet_jsp/irj/root directory, where the server would execute them.

parts.heading: Why patching does not remove it
paragraphs: The vulnerability is only the delivery route. Once the file is on disk, the webshell is a standalone backdoor that needs no exploit, so applying the vendor fix closes the door but leaves anything already planted in place. That is why SANS sees requests for known webshell names like ant.jsp: scanners are checking whether an earlier attacker's shell is still answering, which is cheaper than exploiting the bug again.

Webshells are also commonly used to drop second-stage tools. The Huntress AhsayCBS findings, with cryptominers and a Python command-and-control implant alongside the shells, fit that pattern: the webshell is the foothold, and the follow-on payloads do the long-term work.

parts.heading: What it looks like in telemetry
paragraphs: The strongest endpoint signal is the web server or application server process spawning a command interpreter or reconnaissance tool. On Windows that means processes such as w3wp.exe, or the Java process hosting an application server, launching cmd.exe, powershell.exe, whoami.exe or similar. On Linux, look for the Java or web server process starting sh or bash. In Defender XDR this shows up in DeviceProcessEvents with the server process as InitiatingProcessFileName.

The second signal is script files created in web-served directories by the server process itself, visible in DeviceFileEvents. In web access logs, watch for requests to newly appearing script paths that return success, especially from a small set of source addresses, and for successful POST requests to upload endpoints that should not be reachable from the internet. Many webshells are tiny and evade antivirus signatures, so behavior matters more than file hashes.

parts.heading: Prevention and response
paragraphs: Keep administrative and upload components off the internet where possible, patch exposed application servers quickly, and restrict write permissions so the service account cannot write into executable web directories. File integrity monitoring on web roots catches new script files that signatures miss.

If you find a webshell, treat the host as compromised rather than simply deleting the file. Check for additional shells, scheduled tasks, new accounts, dropped binaries and credential access performed through the shell, and review what that server's service account could reach.

takeaways: Inventory internet-facing SAP NetWeaver Java systems, confirm the CVE-2025-31324 fix is applied, and check whether the Visual Composer metadata uploader is reachable from the internet.
Search the NetWeaver servlet_jsp/irj/root directory and other web roots for JSP, ASPX or PHP files that do not belong to the vendor installation, and compare against a known-good baseline.
Hunt in DeviceProcessEvents for web and application server processes (w3wp.exe, Java-based servers, Apache, nginx) spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, sh, bash, whoami or other recon tools.
Alert in DeviceFileEvents on script files created in web-served directories by the server's own process.
When a webshell is found, scope the whole host for follow-on payloads such as miners, implants, new accounts and scheduled tasks before deciding whether to rebuild.

good_news.headline: Microsoft FORGE Lab finds memory safety bugs in Rust's standard library using agentic tools
good_news.summary: Microsoft Security Blog reports that its FORGE Lab used AI-assisted agentic tools to find and validate several memory safety issues in Rust's standard library, including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The write-up groups the findings into recurring patterns, such as trusting code not to panic and trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, to help others look for similar flaws.
